extracted.intended_audience: patent practitioners (petitioners and patent owners) and counsel participating in PTAB inter partes review proceedings
extracted.subtask_description: A Patent Trial and Appeal Board institution decision addressing whether an inter partes review should be instituted under the AIA; discusses statutory thresholds, evidentiary standards, claim construction approach, real-party-in-interest/privity, and prior-art analyses (anticipation and obviousness).

rubrics_metrics.name: Institution threshold under 35 U.S.C. § 314(a)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inter partes review may not be instituted unless the information presented in the petition “shows that there is a reasonable likelihood that the petitioner would prevail with respect to at least [one] of the claims challenged in the petition.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Findings of fact and conclusions made at institution are preliminary (not final) and are for the sole purpose of determining the institution threshold; any final decision will be based on the full trial record, including any timely Patent Owner response.

rubrics_metrics.name: Time-bar under 35 U.S.C. § 315(b)
rubrics_metrics.description: An inter partes review “may not be instituted if the petition requesting the proceeding is filed more than [one] year after the date on which the petitioner, real party in interest, or privy of the petitioner is served with a complaint alleging infringement of the patent.”
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Petitioners bear the burden of demonstrating compliance with 35 U.S.C. § 312(a)(2) and § 315(b); whether an unnamed entity is a real party-in-interest or in privity is a fact-specific, flexible inquiry (see cited authorities such as Ventex and AIT).

rubrics_metrics.name: Real party-in-interest / privity factors
rubrics_metrics.description: Determination whether an unnamed entity is a real party-in-interest or in privity requires a flexible, fact-dependent approach considering equitable and practical considerations.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors to consider include: (1) an agreement to be bound; (2) pre-existing substantive legal relationships (e.g., preceding/succeeding owners); (3) adequate representation by someone with the same interests; (4) assumption of control over the litigation in which the judgment was rendered; (5) where the nonparty acts as a proxy for the named party to relitigate the same issues; and (6) a special statutory scheme expressly foreclosing successive litigation by nonlitigants (WesternGeco, Taylor, AIT). The relationship must be related to the earlier lawsuit and sufficiently close that the petitioner had a full and fair opportunity to litigate in that earlier lawsuit. Mere existence of some relationship is not sufficient; e.g., generic supplier/customer indemnity agreements, without more, are insufficient to establish privity.

rubrics_metrics.name: Printed publication / public accessibility of prior art
rubrics_metrics.description: A reference qualifies as a printed publication if it was publicly accessible such that persons interested and ordinarily skilled in the subject matter could have located it.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board evaluates evidence of public accessibility (e.g., conference presentations, poster sessions, availability of slides), and a petitioner must meet its burden to show that asserted references are printed publications (the decision here found Sjostrom and Eckberg qualified on this record).

rubrics_metrics.name: Anticipation standard under 35 U.S.C. § 102
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable as anticipated if each and every limitation is found either expressly or inherently in a single prior art reference.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Anticipation requires that all claim elements be disclosed within the four corners of the reference, in a manner enabling one skilled in the art to practice an embodiment of the claimed invention without undue experimentation (Sanofi–Synthelabo; ClearValue).

rubrics_metrics.name: Obviousness standard under 35 U.S.C. § 103 (Graham factors / KSR)
rubrics_metrics.description: A claim is unpatentable under § 103 if the differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art are such that the subject matter as a whole would have been obvious to a person having ordinary skill in the art at the time of the invention.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Resolve obviousness by considering: (1) scope and content of the prior art; (2) differences between the claimed subject matter and the prior art; (3) the level of ordinary skill in the art; and (4) objective evidence of nonobviousness (Graham). KSR governs motivation to combine and predictable results; Board assesses whether a person of ordinary skill would have been motivated to combine teachings and whether the combination yields predictable results.

rubrics_metrics.name: Determination of the level of ordinary skill in the art (POSITA)
rubrics_metrics.description: Level of ordinary skill is determined by considering the state of the art at the relevant time and is important to maintain objectivity in the obviousness inquiry.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Factors include: type of problems encountered in the art; prior art solutions; rapidity with which innovations are made; sophistication of the technology; and educational level of active workers in the field (In re GPAC). On this record the Board adopted Petitioner’s proposed POSITA: at least a bachelor's degree in chemical or mechanical engineering or related field and at least two years' experience implementing pollution control in power generation plants.

rubrics_metrics.name: Claim construction standard (district-court-type / Phillips)
rubrics_metrics.description: In IPRs, claim language is interpreted using the district-court-type standard: give claim terms their ordinary and customary meaning as understood by a person of ordinary skill in the art in light of the claim language, specification, and prosecution history.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Extrinsic evidence may be useful but must be considered in the context of intrinsic evidence (Phillips). The Board construes only terms in controversy and only to the extent necessary to resolve the controversy (37 C.F.R. § 42.100(b); Realtime Data).

rubrics_metrics.name: Waiver for untimely arguments
rubrics_metrics.description: Any arguments not raised by Patent Owner in a timely-filed response may be deemed waived.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Timeliness of responses and the requirement to raise arguments promptly are emphasized to ensure proper development of the trial record and to avoid surprises at later stages.

rubrics_metrics.name: Discretionary denial and multiple petitions (CTPG guidance)
rubrics_metrics.description: The Board has discretion to deny institution of a petition (including lower-ranked petitions) based on considerations such as undue burden and cumulative grounds; the Consolidated Trial Practice Guide recognizes that more than one petition may be necessary when there is a dispute about priority date requiring arguments under multiple prior-art references.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Board considers whether multiple petitions unduly burden the Board or prejudice Patent Owner, whether petitions are cumulative, and whether the circumstances (e.g., priority disputes, different references) justify institution of multiple petitions. The Board may decline to exercise discretion to deny a lower-ranked petition in rare circumstances.

rubrics_metrics.name: Priority entitlement / claim to earlier priority date
rubrics_metrics.description: A patent challenger may need to demonstrate that the challenged patent is not entitled to an asserted earlier priority date to make certain prior art available (e.g., prior art published prior to the later filing date but after earlier priority).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Disputes about priority can affect which references are prior art under § 102; petitions sometimes present alternative priority-date arguments and may justify multiple petitions if priority is in dispute.

rubrics_metrics.name: Evidentiary assessment and burden at institution
rubrics_metrics.description: At the institution stage, the Board determines whether the information in the petition and supporting evidence is sufficient to meet the statutory institution threshold (reasonable likelihood to prevail on at least one claim).
rubrics_metrics.guidance: The Board reviews petitioner’s contentions, declarations, cited references, and any Patent Owner preliminary response; institution findings are preliminary and focused on threshold sufficiency rather than final adjudication. Examples in this decision: sufficiency findings regarding printed publications and the asserted obviousness/anticipation showings.

rubrics_metrics.name: Procedural requirement for sealing and public version
rubrics_metrics.description: After institution, parties have a limited time to file a joint motion to seal the decision and provide a redacted public version.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: No later than fourteen days after issuance of the decision, parties may file a joint motion to seal explaining why the decision should remain under seal and must include a redacted version suitable for public release; the decision remains under seal until the joint motion is resolved and will be made public if no joint motion is filed within the time period.
